prompt.context: Your client is a $1 billion European company with 10 manufacturing sites throughout Europe. One of its key performance measures is 'return on net assets' (RONA), currently at 17%. The company would like to increase this measure to 22%. Its products include thermostats, room controls, switches for microcomputers, and other piece parts for assembly. It sells through five channels: wholesalers (local mom-and-pop stores for DIY home projects), outlets (selling to contractors), construction companies (hotels and restaurants), OEMs (including switches), and manufacturing companies (control processes and refineries).
prompt.question: How should the client increase its return on net assets by 5 percentage points, from 17% to 22%?

clarifying_info.q: What does the competitive landscape look like? How mature are the markets?
clarifying_info.a: Every family of products the client offers is its own market, but all are experiencing average growth — relatively mature markets. The client has two primary competitors.

clarifying_info.q: How do the client's products differ from competitors? Is the product range appropriate?
clarifying_info.a: Products do not differ very much from competitors. Some are more advanced, but all are high quality. The mix seems appropriate — the company makes margins on all products and the range matches what the market wants. The key differentiator is service: the client guarantees delivery within 24–48 hours.

clarifying_info.q: How is the quick-delivery operation structured? Where are the facilities?
clarifying_info.a: The client's 10 production facilities are in Germany, Scotland, France, and Switzerland. Any manufacturing plant delivers all over Europe. The company recently focused its plant operations to achieve economies of scale. Manufactured products are shipped to local affiliates, which store inventory closer to customers to enable quick delivery despite highly variable demand. Despite this recent plant-focusing, the company has not seen an increase in market share. Assume the client cannot achieve additional profits by further consolidating its production facilities.

clarifying_info.q: What are the costs of providing quick delivery?
clarifying_info.a: Operating costs are not a big impact on the cost structure. The significant cost is the working capital tied up in holding stock at local affiliates — estimated at $300 million.

clarifying_info.q: What do competitors spend on delivery? How do their costs compare?
clarifying_info.a: There is no exact information on competitors, but the client believes it is spending more than others due to this working capital issue.

clarifying_info.q: How much do customers actually value the 24–48 hour delivery guarantee?
clarifying_info.a: Through a targeted analysis, the client found that customers are willing to give up speed — the most important thing to them is consistency of delivery, not speed alone. Customers are willing to wait about a week as long as they know the order will arrive on time.

framework: Market overview: size, growth, competitive dynamics across each product family
Product line analysis: differentiation, quality, margins, range appropriateness, key competitive advantage
Three C's — Company (cost structure, working capital, operations), Competition (relative cost position), Customers (what they actually value in delivery)
Identify the strategic mismatch: expensive service that is not valued as-is by customers
Quantify the working capital cost and model the RONA improvement from reducing it
Develop recommendations to realign delivery policy with customer needs and reduce working capital

questions.prompt: Walk through the market and product line. What is the client's competitive position?
questions.guidance: Candidate should note that markets are mature with average growth, two primary competitors, and products that are largely undifferentiated on features. The key differentiator is the 24–48-hour delivery guarantee. Candidate should flag that delivery speed is a strategic bet worth examining.

questions.prompt: Dig into the cost of the quick-delivery strategy. What is the financial drag?
questions.guidance: Candidate should surface that the main cost is not operating expenses but working capital tied up in local affiliate inventory ($300M). Candidate should connect this to the RONA formula: RONA = Net Profit / Net Assets. Holding $300M in working capital inflates net assets, suppressing RONA. Even without a full model, a candidate should articulate that reducing working capital directly improves the denominator of RONA.

math.setup: RONA = Net Income / Net Assets. The $300M in inventory at local affiliates is part of net assets. Saving $200M in working capital reduces net assets. If total assets ~ $2B (implied by 17% RONA on a $1B revenue business), reducing net assets by $200M (10% of total assets) meaningfully lifts RONA. The casebook notes the company saved 10% of total assets.
steps: By reducing stock sites from 10 to 5, client saved ~$200M in working capital
Reducing net assets by 10% while holding net income constant raises RONA proportionally
math.answer: Approximately $200M saved in working capital; represents ~10% reduction in net assets, consistent with the 5pp RONA improvement target (17% → ~22%)

questions.prompt: What does the customer research reveal, and what does it mean strategically?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify the core insight: customers value delivery consistency over delivery speed. A 7–10-day window that is reliable is preferable to a 24–48-hour promise that drives excessive inventory. The client is paying for a capability the customer does not value at that level — a classic strategic misalignment.

brainstorming.prompt: What are the ways a company can improve return on net assets?

categories.name: Increase net income (numerator)
ideas: Improve product mix toward higher-margin items
Expand revenue through new channels or geographies

categories.name: Reduce net assets (denominator)
ideas: Reduce inventory / working capital tied up in the supply chain
Reduce accounts receivable through better collections

categories.name: Operational efficiency
ideas: Rationalize product line to focus on profitable SKUs
Achieve economies of scale through plant consolidation

recommendation: Change the delivery policy from 24–48 hours to 7–10 days, aligned with what customers actually value (consistency over speed)
Centralize inventory by reducing local stock affiliate sites from 10 to 5
Reduce working capital from ~$300M by ~$200M, freeing up capital and improving RONA toward the 22% target
risks: Some customers may have contracts or expectations built around the current 24–48-hour promise — transition needs to be managed carefully
Competitors could attempt to differentiate on delivery speed if the client abandons it
Reducing affiliate sites too aggressively could create delivery inconsistency, undermining the very thing customers care about
next_steps: Conduct customer segmentation to identify any subset that genuinely requires fast delivery and price it as a premium service
Design the optimal affiliate network (site locations, inventory levels) for a 7–10-day consistent delivery model
Develop a transition communication plan for existing customers
Track RONA quarterly against the 22% target as working capital is reduced
